Habits

Why do we eat when we are not hungry?

Eating out of boredom, stress or sadness is very common. Very strict diets sometimes make it worse.

You open the fridge without quite knowing why. You finish a bag of crisps watching a series without having decided to. You crave something sweet right after an upset. Eating is not only a response to hunger.

Physical hunger and emotional hunger

Physical hunger builds gradually, is satisfied by almost any food and goes away once we are full. So-called emotional hunger comes on suddenly, demands specific foods, often sweet or salty, and is not fully satisfied even when we are full. It can be a response to stress, sadness, boredom or tiredness. Eating brings quick relief, and that relief reinforces the habit.

Environmental cues matter too: seeing food, smelling it, having it at hand or associating it with certain moments, such as the sofa in the evening.

The effect of strict diets

The psychologists Janet Polivy and Peter Herman observed in the 1980s that people on very restrictive diets, when they break a rule, tend to eat more than they would have without the diet: the "I've blown it now anyway" reasoning. Rigid restriction can fuel binges.

Plate size rules

Barbara Rolls and her team served the same participants portions of different sizes on different days. With the large portions they ate considerably more, without feeling fuller and without making up for it at later meals. Few people noticed the difference in size. That is why it helps to serve food in the kitchen rather than leaving the dish on the table, and to buy small packs of whatever is hard to stop eating.

Distracted eating

Eating in front of a screen makes us pay less attention to what we eat and to fullness signals. A meta-analysis by Eric Robinson found that distracted eating increases how much is eaten at that moment and, above all, how much is eaten later, perhaps because the earlier meal is remembered less clearly. Eating sitting down, slowly and noticing the taste helps you notice sooner when you have had enough.

What usually helps

  • Pause before eating and ask yourself: am I hungry or is it something else?
  • Find other ways to soothe the emotion: talk to someone, take a walk, have a shower.
  • Do not ban any food completely; instead, eat regularly and without guilt.
  • Change your surroundings: keep impulse foods out of sight.
If you eat large amounts with a sense of losing control, or compensate by vomiting or fasting, see your doctor: it may be an eating disorder, which can be treated.

References

  1. Polivy, J. y Herman, C. P. (1985). Dieting and binging: a causal analysis. American Psychologist, 40(2), 193–201.
  2. van Strien, T. (2018). Causes of emotional eating and matched treatment of obesity. Current Diabetes Reports, 18(6), 35.
  3. Rolls, B. J., Morris, E. L. y Roe, L. S. (2002). Portion size of food affects energy intake in normal-weight and overweight men and women. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 76(6), 1207–1213.
  4. Robinson, E. et al. (2013). Eating attentively: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of food intake memory and awareness on eating. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 97(4), 728–742.
